opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so it's a bit of a winding path. I started my PhD at Ohio State working mostly on biomedical NLP, with Yu Su as my advisor. At the time, GPT-3 had just come out and there was a lot of excitement that in-context learning would just solve everything, including specialized domains. So one of my early projects looked at whether GPT-3 with in-context learning could do biomedical information extraction, things like named entity recognition and relation extraction. What we found was that it really lagged behind much smaller, fine-tuned models like PubMedBERT. That was a humbling result for the "just prompt it" narrative.

That got me thinking about a more fundamental question. In specialized domains like medicine, the knowledge you care about is huge, constantly changing, and often not well represented in pre-training data. So you can't just rely on what's baked into the parameters. You need some way for the model to take in new knowledge and actually use it the way an expert would.

The natural answer was retrieval-augmented generation. But as I worked with RAG, its limitations became pretty clear. Standard RAG encodes each passage independently and retrieves by similarity. That works when the answer sits in one passage, but a lot of real expert reasoning requires connecting pieces of information spread across many documents. Think of a doctor linking a symptom from one paper, a gene from another, and a drug from a third. Vanilla RAG doesn't integrate knowledge across passages. It just finds things that look similar to your query.

Humans are remarkably good at this kind of integration, and that's where the hippocampus came in. I'd been reading about hippocampal memory indexing theory, the idea that the neocortex stores the actual content of memories while the hippocampus maintains an index, a set of associations that points back to those cortical representations. That lets us do pattern completion: from a partial cue, you can recover a whole web of related memories.

So HippoRAG was our attempt to build an analog of that. We use an LLM to turn the corpus into a schemaless knowledge graph, which plays the role of the hippocampal index. At query time, we pull the key concepts from the question and run Personalized PageRank over the graph, so relevance spreads through the associations. That lets us retrieve passages that are connected to the query through multiple hops, in a single retrieval step. On multi-hop QA benchmarks it did really well compared with standard retrievers, and it was much cheaper and faster than iterative retrieval methods.

The deeper motivation, which still drives my work, is long-term memory for these models. How do you build systems that keep learning and integrating new knowledge continually, the way people do, instead of being frozen at pre-training? Specialized domains made that problem concrete for me, and HippoRAG was my first real swing at it.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So my background, going back to my PhD at Ohio State, was really in biomedical NLP. I spent a lot of time thinking about how you get language models to be useful in a domain like medicine, where the knowledge is dense, highly technical, and changes all the time. And one thing that became very clear very early is that you can't just rely on what's in the model's parameters. The pretraining data is a snapshot, it's incomplete for specialized fields, and when the model doesn't know something, it tends to make something up rather than admit it.

So the natural move was retrieval, right? Give the model access to an external knowledge store and let it pull in what it needs. And retrieval-augmented generation works pretty well for the simple case, where the answer is sitting in a single passage and you just need to find it. But in a domain like biomedicine, the interesting questions almost never look like that. A clinician or a researcher is usually connecting things: this gene is associated with this pathway, which is affected by this drug, which has this side effect in patients with this condition. The answer is spread across multiple documents, and none of those documents individually looks like a match for the question.

Standard vector retrieval basically fails there. You embed the question, you embed the passages, you take the nearest neighbors, and you get a bunch of things that are superficially similar to the query but don't actually let you make the connections. People tried to patch that with iterative retrieval, where the model retrieves, reasons, retrieves again, and so on. That helps, but it's slow, it's expensive, and it's fragile, because every step is a chance to drift.

And that's where I started thinking about how humans actually do this. We don't re-read our whole memory every time we need to connect two facts. The hippocampus, in the dominant theory of how long-term memory works, acts as kind of an index over the neocortex. It stores these sparse associations between concepts, and when you get a cue, activation spreads through that index and pulls up the related memories, even if they were encoded at very different times. It's associative, it's single-shot, and it's really good at exactly the multi-hop pattern that was giving us trouble.

So HippoRAG was an attempt to take that structure seriously as an engineering design. We use a language model to read the corpus once and extract entities and relations into a knowledge graph, which plays the role of the hippocampal index. Then at query time, instead of just doing a nearest-neighbor lookup, we identify the entities in the question and run Personalized PageRank over the graph. That spreading-activation step is what lets you reach a passage that's two or three hops away from the question in one retrieval call, with no iterative reasoning loop. And it turned out that gave us both better multi-hop accuracy and a big reduction in cost compared to the iterative approaches.

So really the path was: specialized domains forced me to care about retrieval, retrieval exposed how bad we are at associative, multi-hop questions, and neuroscience happened to have a very clean account of a system that's good at precisely that.

astra-6.text:
The starting point was thinking about how to make language models useful in specialized domains, where a lot of the knowledge you need isn’t necessarily captured in the model’s parameters. You need a way to bring in that knowledge and update it as new information becomes available.

Retrieval-augmented generation is a natural approach: retrieve relevant passages and give them to the model. But that raises another question: what if answering a question requires connecting information across several passages? A passage might be important even if, on its own, it doesn’t look particularly similar to the question.

That led us to think about retrieval as a memory problem. You don’t just want to store individual pieces of information; you want to preserve the connections between them, so a query can bring back a connected set of facts.

That’s the motivation behind HippoRAG. The inspiration is the hippocampus and its role in connecting experiences in memory. We use a language model to help build a knowledge graph from text, and then use those connections during retrieval. The idea is to give the model an external memory that supports association across documents, so it can find the information it needs even when that information is distributed across different sources.

sol-6.1.text:
The question for me was how to make language models useful in specialized domains, where they need knowledge that may not be captured well in their parameters. You can give a model access to documents through retrieval, but then the challenge becomes retrieving the right information when the answer is spread across several sources.

That led us to think about retrieval as more than finding a passage that looks similar to the question. If one passage introduces an entity and another explains a relevant relationship, you need a way to connect them. A knowledge graph gives you a structure for those connections.

That’s the motivation behind HippoRAG: combine the language model’s ability to interpret text with a structured memory that supports associative retrieval. The goal is to bring together the pieces of knowledge the model needs, even when no single passage contains the whole answer.
